HireMe.metaDescription: Get in touch — open to engineering roles, freelance work, and technical collaboration.
HireMe.subtitle: Open to new opportunities, technical collaboration, and interesting conversations.

faqHr.a: Based in Chemnitz, Germany. Open to roles across Germany, the EU, UK, US, UAE, Canada, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, and Australia — remote-first works too.
One month, at my current role with Infineon Technologies.

faqHr.q: Are you open to contract or freelance work?
faqHr.a: Open to full-time contract roles. For freelance work, only through an intermediary/EOR platform like remozo.com.

faqHr.q: What are your long-term career goals?
faqHr.a: I'm working toward German citizenship, so I'm looking for a stable role I can grow in over the next 5 years — ideally at the intersection of distributed systems and AI.
Building Infineon's Parking Guidance System from the ground up — backend, frontend, and the embedded computer vision — replacing a paid vendor and now serving 8,000 users.

faqHr.q: What motivates you to perform well at work?
faqHr.a: Building things that create measurable impact, plus a genuine love of technology — it's what got me into engineering in the first place.

faqHr.q: How do you stay current with industry trends?
faqHr.a: Hands-on experimentation — I hold Anthropic certifications in the Claude API/SDK and Claude Code, and I write the occasional article (the last one hit 5K+ views across Habr, Dev, and Medium).

faqHr.q: Can you give an example of working as part of a team to achieve a goal?
faqHr.a: Leading a 3-person team on the NCahoots admin app at WeDo.agency — I introduced React and set up linting, formatting, and pre-commit hooks to keep quality consistent across the team.

faqHr.q: What do you consider the most important qualities for success?
faqHr.a: Speed — shipping fast and iterating matters more today than getting the design perfect upfront.
Currently targeting €50–70K/year, which also covers the EU Blue Card salary threshold.

faqTech.q: How do you approach code quality and mentoring?
faqTech.a: I set up automated quality gates early — linters, formatters, pre-commit hooks — so code review can focus on design instead of style, and I've mentored several developers along the way.

faqTech.q: Do you have production on-call experience?
faqTech.a: Yes — I've built and operated services handling real traffic at Infineon and OZON Tech, including Kubernetes deployments monitored with Prometheus and Grafana.

faqTech.q: How do you approach architecture decisions?
faqTech.a: Trade-off driven, documented as ADRs — see the Decisions page for real examples from past projects.

faqTech.q: Can I see your code or side projects?
faqTech.a: Check the Skills page for an interactive breakdown of my stack, or Projects for full case studies.

faqTech.q: How do you decide when to refactor vs. rewrite?
faqTech.a: I default to refactor — most systems don't need a rewrite, just the parts that changed most often cleaned up first. A rewrite only makes sense when the architecture itself is the blocker.

faqTech.q: How do you approach system design for scalability?
faqTech.a: Start from real load, not a hypothetical one — at OZON Tech I designed a Go microservice that searches 200M warehouse items in under 5 seconds using ElasticSearch and Kafka, load-tested before it ever shipped.

faqTech.q: What's your approach to incident response?
faqTech.a: Fix first, understand second, prevent third. I've run production on-call at Infineon and OZON Tech with Kubernetes deployments monitored through Prometheus and Grafana, so the goal is catching a regression on a dashboard before a customer does.

faqTech.q: How do you evaluate whether to adopt a new technology?
faqTech.a: I prototype it against a real problem I already have, not a toy example — that's how RAG, LangChain, and MCP earned a place in my stack, and how plenty of other tools didn't.

faqTech.q: How do you handle disagreements about technical direction?
faqTech.a: Write the trade-offs down as an ADR and let the data settle it where possible — most 'disagreements' turn out to be unstated assumptions about priorities.

Tests should catch the failure modes that actually happen in production, not just hit a coverage number — unit tests plus load tests were what let me ship the OZON search service with confidence at 200M-item scale.

faqTech.q: How do you use AI in your development workflow?
faqTech.a: Claude Code paired with TDD — tests are what make AI-generated code trustworthy, not just fast. I'm also familiar with structured agentic workflows like GSD and Superpowers for keeping AI-assisted development disciplined.

faqBusiness.q: Can you work directly with a non-technical founder?
faqBusiness.a: Yes — at WeDo.agency I shipped 9 startup projects working directly with founders, translating business goals into technical scope.

faqBusiness.q: How do you scope an MVP?
faqBusiness.a: I focus on the smallest slice that proves the business hypothesis, then iterate — happy to walk through trade-offs openly.

faqBusiness.q: Are you open to fractional or part-time engagements?
faqBusiness.a: Yes — open to discussing scope, time commitment, and rates directly.

faqBusiness.q: What kind of ROI have you delivered?
faqBusiness.a: €480K/year in savings at Infineon, €86K at OZON Tech, and an 11.63% metric uplift at onlineTours — see the Impact Dashboard for details.

faqBusiness.q: Have you built something from 0 to 1 before?
faqBusiness.a: Yes — I built Infineon's Parking Guidance System from the ground up: backend, frontend, and the embedded computer vision, taking it from an idea to a live system used by 8,000 people.

faqBusiness.q: How comfortable are you wearing multiple hats?
faqBusiness.a: Very — at WeDo.agency I shipped 9 different startup products, often solo, covering backend, frontend, infrastructure, and sometimes the AI/ML pieces too.

faqBusiness.q: How do you operate with ambiguous or incomplete requirements?
faqBusiness.a: I ship the smallest version that tests the real assumption, then let actual usage tell me what to build next — that's how I scope every MVP.

faqBusiness.q: Are you open to equity as part of compensation?
faqBusiness.a: Open to discussing it as part of the overall package, especially for a role with real ownership — happy to talk specifics directly.

faqBusiness.q: What's your risk tolerance for joining an early-stage company?
faqBusiness.a: I've spent a year at WeDo.agency shipping fast for early-stage clients, so I'm comfortable with the pace — that said, I'm currently looking for a role I can commit to long-term.

faqBusiness.q: How do you move fast without breaking things?
faqBusiness.a: Automate the guardrails instead of skipping them — I've gotten CI/CD pipelines down to under 10 seconds per deploy, which means shipping quickly without losing the safety net.

scalingSim.title: Why the point-update service was the real bet
scalingSim.description: The barcode scanners themselves weren't the hard part — routing them through a shared service instead of wiring each one into a single app was. Drag the slider to see why that choice matters as load grows.
scalingSim.hint: Drag the slider to change user count.
scalingSim.verticalImpossible: No single machine exists at this scale
scalingSim.nodesTemplate: {count, plural, one {# commodity node} other {# commodity nodes}}
scalingSim.ratioTemplate: At this load, horizontal scaling costs {ratio}× less than the single machine that would be needed to match it.
scalingSim.ratioImpossible: At this load, no single machine can do the job at all — only horizontal scaling works.
scalingSim.ratioNone: At this load, vertical and horizontal cost about the same — the gap only opens up as load grows.
scalingSim.strategicNote: That's the real strategic payoff of this project: the old setup wired each barcode scanner directly into one legacy app, so shipping a new interface would have meant buying new scanner hardware. Routing scans through a shared point-update service decoupled the two — new terminals and app interfaces plug into the same backend, which scales out with commodity nodes instead of needing an ever-bigger central server.

parkingGuidance.title: How a free spot reaches the map
parkingGuidance.description: Step through the path of one occupancy update — or see what happens when a camera goes dark.

onDevice.label: On-device vision
onDevice.detail: C firmware · plate recognition + occupancy count

backend.label: Backend
backend.detail: Python CV service · C# device layer

occupancy.label: A car parks
steps: A camera built on Infineon's own PSoC Edge chip watches a row of parking spots on the Dresden campus.
Firmware written in C runs the computer vision on the chip itself — number-plate recognition and occupancy counting — instead of sending video to a model in the cloud.

Only the result leaves the camera: a small occupancy event over MQTT. No video crosses the network, which keeps bandwidth low and avoids storing footage centrally. MQTT was picked over HTTP polling to keep latency under 500 ms.
Backend services take the event: a Python service works out which spots are free, and a C# layer handles device auth, provisioning and the REST/WebSocket API.
The React dashboard gets the update over a WebSocket and repaints the campus map in real time.

offline.label: A camera goes offline
steps: A camera drops off the network and its events stop.
The backend doesn't keep serving the last numbers it saw.
The map marks that zone as "unknown" — honest uncertainty instead of stale data telling drivers a spot is free.

parkingGuidance.note: Simplified: the real system covers several lots and camera types. Each lot's layout is configuration data, so adding a lot means adding a JSON file, not changing code.

warehouseSearch.title: What happens when a picker searches
warehouseSearch.description: Compare a cached search, an uncached one, and how a catalog change reaches the index.

hit.label: Popular SKU
steps: A picker types a SKU — in Cyrillic or Latin, e.g. "БОЛТ М8" or "bolt m8".
The warehouse management web app sends the query to the search service over REST.
The Go service handles bursts of concurrent terminals from one small, single-binary deployment.
Cache hit: the 10,000 most-searched SKUs sit in Redis, so common queries return in about 40 ms at P95 instead of about 800 ms.

miss.label: Rare SKU
steps: A picker types a SKU — in Cyrillic or Latin, e.g. "БОЛТ М8" or "bolt m8".
The warehouse management web app sends the query to the search service over REST.
The Go service handles bursts of concurrent terminals from one small, single-binary deployment.
Cache miss: this SKU isn't one of the hot ones in Redis.

ElasticSearch runs full-text and fuzzy search over 200M items. A custom analyzer matches the Cyrillic and Latin spellings of the same SKU. Result: under 5 seconds, where the old SQL LIKE query had become unusable.

update.label: Catalog changes
steps: A product changes in the catalog.
The change is published to Kafka, so nothing has to poll the database.
The search service consumes the event.
It updates the ElasticSearch index. Searches see the change within about 2 seconds.
The same events invalidate cached entries. Lesson learned: a short TTL as a backstop — a batch update once caused a cache-miss storm.

warehouseSearch.note: Prometheus and Grafana track P50/P95/P99 latency, cache hit rate and Kafka consumer lag; Jaeger traces individual queries.

semanticSearch.title: Follow a question through the pipeline
semanticSearch.description: The search UI streams each of these stages live over Server-Sent Events. Switch to see how the open data got in first.

search.label: Search
steps: Someone asks a question in plain language. The UI opens a Server-Sent Events stream and renders each stage as it arrives.
The FastAPI orchestrator fans the query out.

An embedding model turns it into a dense vector — bge-m3, multilingual-e5-base, jina-embeddings-v3 or LaBSE, all behind the same /embed contract. A model-independent sparse vector is computed too, via a hashing trick, so every model can be compared on equal terms.
Qdrant runs dense and sparse search together and merges both rankings with reciprocal rank fusion — exact keywords and acronyms in dataset titles aren't lost.

jina-reranker-v3 re-scores just the top candidates, reading query and document together: slower per item, more accurate on a short list. It falls back from CUDA to MPS to CPU, and halves its batch size instead of crashing when memory runs out.
An LLM runs multi-query expansion and writes a plain-language interpretation of the results.
Datasets and interpretation stream back to the UI, stage by stage.

ingest.label: Ingest open data
steps: Berlin, Chemnitz, Dresden and Leipzig each publish open data on their own portal.
A separate Playwright scraper per city walks that city's dataset catalog.
Datasets are stored in Qdrant as named dense and sparse vectors.
The rest of each dataset's record lives in MongoDB.

semanticSearch.note: The thesis's research contribution is the benchmark: every model × search mode × multi-query combination, scored by weighted relevance and by the share of results rated relevant.

newsAggregator.title: Inside the news aggregator
newsAggregator.description: Three paths through the system: harvesting feeds, reading the news on a map, and adding a source.

harvest.label: Harvest
steps: On an interval, a gocron job wakes up inside the Go backend.
It reads the registered publishers and their RSS sources from PostgreSQL, the source of truth.
It pulls the new articles from each feed.
New articles are indexed in ElasticSearch for full-text search.

read.label: Read the news
steps: A reader filters by date histogram, category, country and language — country also from a clickable world map — and can use AND / EXACT / NOT operators.
The Next.js site calls the Go API over REST through RTK Query.
ElasticSearch runs the full-text query; a denormalized publisher index powers autocomplete.
Results appear on a Yandex Maps view, placed by their publishers' coordinates.

admin.label: Add a source
steps: An editor signs in to the separate Next.js admin app. The public site never ships admin code.
The Go API checks the JWT.
The new publisher or RSS source is saved to PostgreSQL, and the next harvest picks it up.

newsAggregator.note: Observability from the first endpoint: logs in ELK, traces in Jaeger, metrics in Prometheus/Grafana. Every push to main redeploys the Docker Compose stack.

telegramBots.title: From ad tap to AI conversation
telegramBots.description: How a user arrived in the bot, and what happened when they sent a voice message.

funnel.label: Ad funnel
steps: Someone taps a Meta ad for one of the characters.

Facebook's ad policy penalizes landing pages that prompt a download, and Telegram's default t.me page has an app-download button. So the team self-hosted a stripped-down clone that keeps only the deep link into the bot.
The deep link opens the bot, built in Python with aiogram on PostgreSQL.
Keitaro records the conversion…
…and reports it back to Meta, so cost per lead was measured accurately.

voice.label: Voice message
steps: A user records a voice message to the psychologist character.
Whisper transcribes it — this is what let people talk instead of type.
The scripted AI character answers in role.
The reply lands back in the chat; Redis holds the user's state between messages.

telegramBots.note: Deploys ran on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner with Docker layer caching — about 10 seconds each.

semki.title: Finding the right colleague
semki.description: First the profiles get indexed, then anyone can ask in plain language.

index.label: Index profiles
steps: Employee profiles describe who works on what, across siloed departments.
The OpenAI API turns each profile into an embedding.
Embeddings go into Qdrant for vector search.

ask.label: Ask
steps: Someone asks in plain language who could help with a topic.
The Go API (Gin) receives the question.
Repeated questions are answered from the Redis cache.
Otherwise the OpenAI API embeds the question.
Qdrant returns the closest profiles; they become the retrieved context for a RAG-style answer.
The React app shows the relevant colleagues.

semki.note: Built at a hackathon but observed like production: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Jaeger on Kubernetes.

fassonApi.title: FaceID-style sign-in, step by step
fassonApi.description: The same webcam capture serves two flows: registering a face, and signing in with it.

register.label: Register
steps: The browser grabs a single webcam frame over WebRTC.
It's posted to the ASP.NET MVC backend.
Azure's Face API detects the face in the frame.
The portrait is stored in Azure Blob Storage.

login.label: Sign in
steps: The browser grabs a single webcam frame over WebRTC.
It's posted to the ASP.NET MVC backend.
Azure's Face API detects the face and matches it.
On a match, the user is signed in.

firebaseSlack.title: From signup to Slack message
firebaseSlack.description: What the extension does every time someone creates an account.

signup.label: Signup
steps: Someone signs up in an app that has the extension installed.
Firebase Auth fires a user-creation event.
That event triggers the extension's TypeScript Cloud Function.
The function fills in the message template configured at install time.
It posts to the Slack webhook URL from the configuration, and the team sees the signup right away.

firebaseSlack.note: Published on extensions.dev and installed in 90 projects: set the webhook URL and template once, nothing to maintain.

subwayBattery.description: Readings flow in from the trains; a rebalancing command flows out.

telemetry.label: Live readings

The readings are sent over a cellular connection.
The Angular admin panel shows all 30 units' live readings.

rebalance.label: Rebalance

The panel calls the backend's command endpoint.

colorRobot.title: How the robot names a color

object.label: Colored object
object.detail: held in front of the sensor

known.label: Known color
steps: An object is held in front of the robot.
The TCS3200 sensor reads its color.
The Arduino Uno classifies the reading as one of 13 named colors.
Each color has its own buzzer tone, so the robot answers with sound.

unknown.label: Unknown color
steps: An object is held in front of the robot.
The TCS3200 sensor reads its color.
The reading matches none of the 13 colors.
An LED lights up instead of a tone.

lightning.title: Draw a table, get the SQL
lightning.description: Edit the entity the way you would on the Lightning canvas — the CREATE TABLE statement rewrites itself as you type.
lightning.note: This live table-to-SQL step was the part of the zero-code idea that actually worked. Relation SQL and mock data stayed stubs; the request-tree panel exported a real Postman collection.

swe.title: Draw a table, get the SQL
swe.description: Same idea as the coursework: edit the entity and the CREATE TABLE statement regenerates live.
swe.note: Like the original, this only writes SQL — there is no database connection, nothing is executed.

parallax.title: How a flat picture becomes 2.5D
parallax.description: The editor splits an illustration into layers and gives each a depth. Tilting the phone shifts every layer in proportion to its depth — far layers barely move, near ones move most.
parallax.stageAria: Layered landscape illustration that shifts with pointer movement or device tilt
parallax.hintPointer: Move the pointer over the picture (or drag across it) to simulate tilting the device.
parallax.note: The original 2020 hackathon prototype was a single vanilla-JS page using parallax.js; the editor rebuilt it so artists could prepare their own layered pieces.
